paragraphs: Clustering assigns examples to groups without starting from known class labels. This paper proposes choosing those assignments by maximizing statistical dependence between the input variables and the assigned cluster labels. It measures that dependence with the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, or HSIC. The central idea is that a useful grouping should have a strong statistical relationship with the data it describes.

This objective brings several perspectives on clustering into one framework. Geometric approaches emphasize the arrangement of points, spectral approaches use matrix-based representations, and dependence-based approaches emphasize statistical relationships. The authors show that their framework includes many existing algorithms, including k-means and spectral clustering, as special cases. This provides a common language for methods that otherwise appear different.

A distinctive feature is that kernels can describe the cluster labels as well as the inputs, allowing particular structures to be imposed on the labels. The paper also derives a perturbation bound for changes in k-means clustering. Together, these contributions connect the design of clustering objectives with an analysis of how clustering can change under perturbations.
icml-2007-a-dependence-maximization-view.tldr: The paper unifies several clustering methods by maximizing statistical dependence between data and cluster labels.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a method for learning causal directions by measuring how strongly variables depend on one another. Its dependence measure uses kernel-based cross-covariance operators and their Hilbert-Schmidt norm. In plain language, the method turns statistical relationships into numerical strengths that can be compared when assessing possible causal explanations.

The central assumption concerns what happens after conditioning on another variable. If conditioning on Z increases the dependence between X and Y, the method treats this as evidence that Z is likely to be a common effect of X and Y. The abstract relates this assumption to the faithfulness perspective used in constraint-based causal learning. It is an assumption guiding causal interpretation, rather than an unconditional rule that dependence changes establish causation.

The algorithm gathers votes for candidate causal directions from these comparisons and orients edges according to the majority. In most experiments with known causal structures, it produced plausible results and outperformed the conventional PC algorithm. Those findings support the usefulness of aggregating dependence-strength evidence in the tested settings while preserving the method's reliance on its stated causal assumption.
icml-2007-a-kernel-based-causal-learning.tldr: A kernel-based causal learner uses changes in dependence to vote on causal directions under an explicit common-effect assumption.

paragraphs: This paper studies incremental classification algorithms that resemble the Perceptron but explicitly pursue a large margin. A margin describes how confidently a separating boundary places examples on their assigned sides. The authors introduce a family of algorithms whose behavior is governed by the number of mistakes made during learning, using rules that involve powers of that count.

Two parts of learning follow these rules: the effective learning rate and the condition that determines misclassification. The effective learning rate is the ordinary learning rate divided by the length of the weight vector. Controlling this ratio connects the size of an update to the current scale of the classifier, while controlling the misclassification condition shapes when an update is triggered.

The authors examine when these algorithms converge after finitely many steps. Under conditions described as relatively mild, they identify a parameter limit in which convergence yields a maximum-margin classifier. This is a conditional limiting result, not a claim that every parameter choice reaches the maximum margin. The paper also presents experimental comparisons with other large-margin Perceptron-like algorithms and decomposition SVM solvers.
icml-2007-approximate-maximum-margin-alg.tldr: Mistake-count rules control incremental classifiers that approach maximum-margin classification in a parameter limit under stated conditions.

paragraphs: This paper develops a linear classifier for examples represented as matrices. Its main contribution is a regularization scheme based on the spectral ℓ₁ norm of the classifier's coefficient matrix. The regularizer controls model complexity while also allowing the rank of that coefficient matrix to be determined automatically, linking prediction with the discovery of a lower-dimensional structure.

The authors formulate the inference task as one convex optimization problem using linear matrix inequalities. This brings the classification objective and spectral regularization into a single optimization framework. The rank is therefore addressed as part of fitting the classifier rather than being treated only as a separate representation choice.

In an application to motor-imagery EEG classification, the method improves classification performance over conventional methods. It also identifies a signal subspace that concentrates information useful for discrimination, without requiring an additional feature-extraction step. The abstract further states that changing the loss function extends the approach to regression. The contribution thus combines matrix classification, complexity control, and discriminative subspace identification within one formulation.
icml-2007-classifying-matrices-with-a-sp.tldr: Spectral regularization lets a matrix classifier control complexity and determine coefficient rank while improving motor-imagery EEG classification.

paragraphs: Transfer learning aims to use experience from a source task to accelerate learning on a target task. In reinforcement learning, the paper notes that promising existing transfer methods typically operate between very similar tasks. It asks whether knowledge can also be useful when the source and target belong to different domains.

The proposed algorithm, Rule Transfer, first learns rules that summarize the source task's policy: the behavior learned for choosing actions. It then uses those rules to help learning in the target task. The rule summary is the intermediate form through which experience is transferred, allowing the method to carry policy knowledge from one task into another.

The authors demonstrate transfer from gridworld tasks to Keepaway, a robot-soccer reinforcement-learning benchmark. Their experiments show that this source experience can speed learning in Keepaway, with effectiveness assessed through three distinct transfer metrics. The significance is the demonstrated cross-domain transfer: a policy summary learned in gridworld can assist learning in the tested soccer setting. The result establishes effectiveness for those experiments rather than a guarantee for arbitrary domain pairs.
icml-2007-cross-domain-transfer-for-rein.tldr: Rule Transfer summarizes a learned policy as rules and uses them to accelerate learning from gridworld experience to robot soccer.

paragraphs: Classification becomes difficult when examples have many input dimensions but only a small training set is available. The paper starts from the possibility that accurate prediction may still be achievable if the data occupy a low-dimensional manifold. A useful representation would capture that smaller underlying space while retaining the information needed to distinguish classes.

Gaussian Process Latent Variable Models can discover low-dimensional manifolds from relatively few examples, but their usual latent representation does not account for class labels. Other discriminative manifold-learning methods constrain how classes are arranged, yet the abstract notes that their generally deterministic formulations may generalize poorly with limited training data. These observations motivate combining latent-space learning with explicit class information.

The proposed method performs Gaussian process classification using latent-variable models trained with discriminative priors over the latent space. Those priors guide the hidden representation toward distinctions relevant to classification. The stated contribution is the ability to learn a discriminative latent space from a small training set, addressing the joint need for dimensionality reduction and label-aware representation learning.
icml-2007-discriminative-gaussian-proces.tldr: Discriminative priors guide a Gaussian process latent-variable model toward class-relevant representations from small training sets.

paragraphs: Graphs can represent objects such as chemical compounds and XML documents, but turning them into features creates a major size problem. One possible representation records whether each possible subgraph pattern is present. Because the collection of possible patterns is enormous, the resulting binary feature space can become too large for ordinary statistical methods.

This paper proposes selecting a small set of salient patterns by tracking a regularization path. The approach connects pattern selection with changes in regularization, which controls how complex the selected representation can become. Crucially, it expands the pattern search space progressively, minimizing the generation of patterns that will prove useless.

The computational strategy therefore addresses both which patterns to retain and how much of the possible pattern space to generate. Experiments show considerably greater efficiency than a simpler approach based on frequent substructure mining. The stated finding supports the value of coordinating pattern generation with regularization-based selection, rather than treating the huge collection of candidate graph features as something that must all be available in advance.
icml-2007-entire-regularization-paths-fo.tldr: Regularization-path tracking selects salient graph patterns while progressively expanding the search space to reduce unnecessary pattern generation.

paragraphs: Graph clustering seeks groups whose relationships are expressed through links in a network. This paper examines two approaches: a new graph adaptation of k-medoids and the Girvan-Newman method, which uses edge betweenness centrality. The authors show that both can uncover latent communities defined by graph connectivity, making them useful for relational data.

Their obstacle is computational cost. The operations needed by these approaches can become prohibitively expensive for large relational datasets. The paper brings in network structure indices, an existing technique for indexing network structure and finding short paths efficiently. Incorporating these indices into the clustering algorithms targets the expensive graph computations that restrict their practical use.

The authors show how this incorporation can overcome the identified complexity limitations and evaluate the modified methods on synthetic and real datasets. They describe the quantitative and qualitative results as promising. The contribution is thus an efficiency-oriented adaptation of useful clustering ideas, supported by evidence about both measured behavior and the communities produced, rather than a claim that every network will yield equally strong results.
icml-2007-graph-clustering-with-network-.tldr: Network structure indices reduce expensive graph computations in two community-detection methods, with promising evaluations on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems produce structures rather than single labels, and the appropriate graphical model can depend on the output being constructed. This paper introduces Incremental Sigmoid Belief Networks, or ISBNs, for that situation. The challenge is to accommodate changing model structure without having to sum over all possible model structures.

ISBNs address this through directed connections and an incremental specification of the model. Building the structure progressively avoids that particular summation, but exact inference in the resulting directed models remains intractable. The authors therefore derive two efficient approximations based on mean field methods, providing practical ways to use the proposed model class.

Both approximations prove effective in artificial experiments and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on a benchmark natural-language parsing task. The approximation that more closely resembles an ISBN also gives better parsing accuracy. This comparison suggests that the underlying ISBN formulation captures useful aspects of structure prediction. It supports the model's suitability in the studied setting, while the practical results depend on approximate rather than exact inference.
icml-2007-incremental-bayesian-networks-.tldr: Incremental Bayesian networks build model structure alongside predicted structure, with efficient approximations achieving strong parsing results.

paragraphs: Relational learning works with examples described through relationships rather than just flat lists of attributes. This paper presents a kernel for ordered hypergraphs, a representation that captures relational data of the kind used in Inductive Logic Programming. The kernel supplies a way to compare such structured examples for learning.

The similarity calculation is based on walks through a hypergraph and generalizes earlier graph-kernel approaches. Its role is to translate relational structure into comparisons between examples, allowing the chosen representation to contribute directly to learning. The contribution combines a relational data formalization with a corresponding method for measuring similarity.

Experiments on challenging chemical datasets show performance better than existing Inductive Logic Programming methods and competitive with state-of-the-art graph kernels. The experiments also reveal that changing how graph data are encoded can dramatically affect performance. This second finding matters when interpreting the first: the representation of the chemical structures is itself consequential. The authors identify this encoding effect as potentially useful beyond kernel methods, making representation choice an additional lesson of the study.
icml-2007-learning-from-interpretations-.tldr: A walk-based kernel for ordered hypergraphs performs strongly on chemical data and shows that graph encoding can substantially affect results.

paragraphs: This paper uses probability theory to guide searches that must prove whether a player can achieve a goal in an adversarial game. It treats the game tree as a graphical model, producing a distribution over the eventual yes-or-no result before the search finishes. That distribution then guides a best-first search algorithm.

In Go experiments, this probabilistic search explores a similar number of nodes to Proof-Number Search. The authors then incorporate domain knowledge through models that assign prior distributions to the values of leaf nodes. These leaves stand in for portions of the game tree that have not yet been explored, so the priors express expectations about unresolved parts of the proof.

The parameters of those domain-specific models can be learned from earlier search trees. Experiments on Go show that this learned knowledge can increase problem-solving speed by orders of magnitude. The abstract explicitly cautions that overfitting must be avoided. The major gain therefore comes from learning useful guidance for future searches, with the quality of that learned guidance remaining important.
icml-2007-learning-to-solve-game-trees-7.tldr: Probabilistic game-tree search can learn guidance from earlier searches and achieve orders-of-magnitude speedups on Go problems, with care against overfitting.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines several kernel matrices within a learning problem. The paper begins with an existing iterative approach that made large-scale multiple kernel learning practical by reusing support vector machine software. Its remaining drawback is that reaching a reasonable solution can require several iterations, motivating a more efficient formulation and solver.

The authors formulate the problem through adaptive 2-norm regularization. They include weights for the kernel matrices directly in the standard SVM empirical-risk objective and impose an ℓ₁ constraint to encourage sparsity. This makes the relative contributions of the kernels part of the optimization while favoring a solution that uses fewer of them.

The paper proposes an algorithm for this formulation and shows that it is equivalent to approaches based on block 1-norm regularization. That equivalence connects two ways of understanding multiple kernel learning, alongside the practical algorithmic contribution. Experiments report rapid convergence and efficiency that compares favorably with other multiple kernel learning algorithms. These results support the proposed solver as a practical improvement in the tested settings.
icml-2007-more-efficiency-in-multiple-ke.tldr: An adaptive regularization formulation yields an efficient multiple-kernel solver and connects it to block 1-norm regularization.

paragraphs: This paper develops density models in which several hidden, continuous factors jointly explain the observed data. The motivation is to represent different sources of variation separately, as suggested by separating style from content. The proposed construction generalizes multilinear models by introducing nonlinear basis functions, allowing a richer relationship between the hidden factors and observations.

By marginalizing over the weights, the authors obtain a multifactor version of a Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model. Each factor is kernelized independently, so the mapping from an individual factor to the data can be nonlinear. The model therefore preserves separate factors while allowing each to influence the observations through more flexible mappings.

The application is human locomotion. Each pose is modeled through factors representing the person's identity, gait, and current state of motion. The authors demonstrate the approach through time-series prediction and the synthesis of new animation. These demonstrations show how the factorized model can support both predicting motion over time and generating poses within an animation, connecting its probabilistic formulation to concrete uses.
icml-2007-multifactor-gaussian-process-m.tldr: A multifactor Gaussian process model separates hidden sources of variation and demonstrates motion prediction and novel animation synthesis.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification when objects are accessible only through their pairwise dissimilarities. There are no feature vectors to use directly. The theoretical question is what properties of a dissimilarity function are sufficient to support accurate classifiers, allowing learning to proceed from relationships between objects.

The authors derive sufficient conditions that accommodate unbounded dissimilarities and remain invariant under order-preserving transformations. This means the results do not require a fixed upper limit on dissimilarity values and are unchanged by transformations that preserve their ordering. The theory suggests building an ensemble of decision stumps, each depending on a pair of examples, and combining them with a convex weighting to obtain a large margin.

Guided by that construction, the paper introduces Dissimilarity based Boosting, or DBoost. Experiments across several databases and different conditions show that it compares favorably with existing approaches. The work links a theoretical account of when dissimilarity information can suffice with a practical ensemble method. Its conditions are sufficient for the stated learning results, rather than presented as requirements every useful dissimilarity must satisfy.
icml-2007-on-learning-with-dissimilarity.tldr: DBoost turns pairwise dissimilarities into a large-margin ensemble, guided by sufficient conditions for learning without feature vectors.

paragraphs: Learning methods that keep tracking a solution are often associated with environments that change over time. This paper challenges the idea that tracking matters only in such settings. It presents three results suggesting that continued adaptation can also be valuable when the learning problem is stationary.

The first result uses a simple example called the Black and White problem, where tracking can outperform any converging algorithm. The second demonstrates the same point in a larger application of temporal-difference learning to computer Go. These results establish that stationarity alone does not make convergence the preferable behavior in every learning problem.

The third result examines meta-learning through IDBD, an algorithm that adapts step sizes. On the Black and White problem, this adaptation has a dramatic long-term effect, whereas an analogous converging problem shows only a small, second-order effect. The authors cautiously suggest that stationary tracking problems could help research on learning to learn, feature selection, and transfer. In particular, they see a possible route toward choosing meta-learning tasks through an independent methodology.
icml-2007-on-the-role-of-tracking-in-sta.tldr: Examples show that tracking can outperform convergence even in stationary problems and suggest useful directions for meta-learning task selection.

paragraphs: The paper considers a sequential assignment problem: repeatedly choose a map that assigns elements of one set to a few elements of another. Each choice incurs a cost. The objective is to keep the accumulated loss close to that of the best single map chosen with knowledge of the entire sequence.

Finding that best map offline is provably hard. The authors introduce Randomized Map Prediction, or RMP, as an efficient online approximation that performs nearly as well. The method draws on prediction with expert advice, connecting sequential choices among mappings to a broader framework for learning from the performance of alternatives.

RMP also provides an online approach to problems usually treated as batch tasks, where all data are processed together. The authors apply it to online clustering and online feature selection. In their experiments, it often outperforms standard batch algorithms on those problems. This empirical result is separate from the approximation claim: the paper offers both a theoretically motivated sequential method and evidence that its online formulation can be practically competitive.
icml-2007-online-discovery-of-similarity.tldr: Randomized Map Prediction efficiently learns sequential assignments and often outperforms standard batch methods in clustering and feature-selection experiments.

paragraphs: Pegasos is an iterative solver for the optimization problem behind support vector machines. It alternates stochastic gradient descent steps with projection steps. The paper analyzes this simple procedure and proves an iteration requirement of Õ(1/ε) for accuracy ε, compared with Ω(1/ε²) in previous analyses of stochastic gradient descent methods.

The iteration count also scales linearly with the inverse of the SVM regularization parameter λ. For a linear kernel, the stated total runtime is Õ(d/(λε)), where d bounds the number of nonzero features in each example. The runtime bound does not depend directly on the number of training examples, making the method especially relevant to large datasets with sparse examples.

The approach can also use nonlinear kernels while continuing to optimize the primal objective. Experiments on large text-classification problems compare Pegasos with existing state-of-the-art SVM solvers. One reported RCV1 problem contains 800,000 training examples and takes less than five seconds to converge. This concrete result illustrates the solver's efficiency in the reported setting alongside its theoretical scaling analysis.
icml-2007-pegasos-primal-estimated-sub-g.tldr: Pegasos combines stochastic gradient and projection steps to solve SVMs with favorable accuracy scaling and strong large-text-dataset performance.

paragraphs: Training a discriminative graphical model can be expensive when each variable has many possible values, even if the graph itself permits tractable computation. Pseudolikelihood is appealing because its running time grows linearly with the number of values per variable. However, the paper notes that its accuracy can be poor on some data.

Piecewise training offers another tradeoff: it can improve accuracy, but its cost scales less favorably with the number of possible values. The authors introduce piecewise pseudolikelihood to combine useful properties of these approaches. The proposed training method retains pseudolikelihood's computational efficiency while allowing substantially better predictive accuracy.

On several natural-language-processing benchmarks, piecewise pseudolikelihood achieves better accuracy than standard pseudolikelihood. In many cases, its accuracy is nearly equivalent to maximum-likelihood training, while training takes five to ten times less time than batch CRF training. These findings show a favorable speed–accuracy tradeoff on the evaluated tasks. They support an efficient alternative when large variable cardinalities make conventional training costly, without asserting that the accuracy match holds in every case.
icml-2007-piecewise-pseudolikelihood-for.tldr: Piecewise pseudolikelihood improves on standard pseudolikelihood accuracy while substantially reducing training time relative to batch CRFs on NLP benchmarks.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering uses patterns in data such as users' movie ratings to make predictions. This paper addresses the difficulty of handling very large rating datasets with existing approaches. It shows how Restricted Boltzmann Machines, a class of two-layer undirected graphical models, can represent tabular data of this kind.

The authors provide efficient procedures for both learning the models and using them for inference. They demonstrate the approach on the Netflix dataset, which contains more than 100 million user–movie ratings. This application establishes that the proposed modeling and computational procedures can operate successfully at the scale of that dataset.

The reported RBM models slightly outperform carefully tuned singular-value-decomposition models. A larger improvement comes from linearly combining predictions from multiple RBMs and multiple SVD models: the combined predictor achieves an error score well over 6% better than Netflix's own system. These are distinct findings. The individual RBMs deliver a modest advantage over the tuned SVD comparison, while the stronger reported improvement belongs to the combined ensemble.
icml-2007-restricted-boltzmann-machines-.tldr: RBMs scale to the Netflix ratings dataset, slightly beat tuned SVD models, and contribute to a stronger combined predictor.

paragraphs: An unusual measurement may reflect an interesting object or simply measurement error. This paper develops a mixture-based model for multivariate experimental data that explicitly includes measurement-error information. Its aim is to identify atypical observations whose unusualness is not explained by those errors, making them candidates for further scientific interest.

Exact inference is not possible in the proposed model, so the authors develop a tree-structured variational expectation-maximization solution. This approximation compares favorably with a fully factorial approximation and approaches the accuracy of Markov-Chain-EM while retaining computational simplicity. The inference method is therefore central to making the richer uncertainty-aware model usable.

Experiments show improved outlier-detection rates when measurement errors are included, across varying levels of measurement uncertainty. The authors also apply the method to an astrophysical survey, using photometric observations and their errors to detect peculiar quasars. The result illustrates why the distinction matters: outlier detection is more useful when it can account for observational uncertainty while searching for objects with potentially interesting intrinsic properties.
icml-2007-robust-mixtures-in-the-presenc.tldr: A mixture model incorporates measurement uncertainty to improve detection of potentially interesting outliers, including peculiar quasars.

paragraphs: This paper recasts decision-tree learning in a compression setting and derives tight bounds on generalization error. Generalization error concerns how a learned classifier performs beyond its training examples. The compression perspective provides a way to analyze that risk through the information used to specify the learned classifier.

The authors develop both sample-compression bounds and Occam's Razor bounds. They describe these bounds as more general than bounds based on VC dimension or Rademacher complexities. A further feature is their ability to support a tradeoff between margin and sparsity, allowing these aspects of a classifier to be balanced in obtaining better classifiers.

The proposed bounds therefore have a potential role beyond assessing a completed tree. They could guide model selection by comparing candidate models through their risk bounds. The authors also suggest that this could replace traditional pruning strategies, which simplify decision trees. That replacement is presented as a possibility, not as an established outcome. The core contribution is the compression-based analysis and the decision-making possibilities it opens for tree learning.
icml-2007-sample-compression-bounds-for-.tldr: Compression-based generalization bounds for decision trees support margin–sparsity tradeoffs and could guide model selection instead of pruning.

paragraphs: Self-taught learning uses unlabeled data to help a supervised classification task without assuming that the unlabeled examples share the labeled data's classes or generative distribution. This broadens the possible source material: the motivating examples include images, audio, and text collected from the Internet, where abundant unlabeled data may be easier to obtain than task-specific examples.

The proposed approach uses sparse coding to learn higher-level features from that unlabeled material. These features then provide a compact representation for the classification task. The transferred knowledge is therefore a representation learned from the additional data, allowing the supervised learner to benefit without requiring labels for those examples.

The authors report that the resulting features significantly improve classification performance. They also show how to learn a Fisher kernel for the representation when classification uses an SVM. The contribution combines a broader setting for learning from unlabeled data with a concrete feature-learning method. Removing the shared-distribution assumption expands where the framework can be considered; it does not assert that every unrelated collection will improve every classifier.
icml-2007-self-taught-learning-transfer-.tldr: Self-taught learning uses sparse coding on unlabeled data to improve classification without assuming matching classes or data distributions.

paragraphs: Core vector machines scale kernel methods through a geometric formulation based on a minimum enclosing ball. Although the idea is simple, an efficient implementation still needs a sophisticated numerical solver. This paper changes the geometric problem to reduce that implementation burden while retaining a useful connection to the original formulation.

The proposed enclosing-ball problem fixes the radius instead of minimizing it. The authors develop efficient algorithms with a (1 + ε) approximation guarantee that are simple to implement and require no numerical solver. For the Gaussian kernel, they show that a suitable fixed radius is easy to choose and that the resulting approximate center is close to the corresponding minimum-enclosing-ball center.

Experiments report accuracy comparable to other large-scale SVM implementations, an ability to handle very large datasets, and generally faster operation than the core vector machine. The results support fixed-radius enclosing balls as a practical simplification. The geometric closeness statement is specifically described for the Gaussian-kernel setting, while the speed and accuracy comparisons are findings from the reported experiments.
icml-2007-simpler-core-vector-machines-w.tldr: Fixing the enclosing-ball radius yields simpler kernel-learning algorithms with approximation guarantees and competitive large-scale SVM results.

paragraphs: Many learning methods depend on eigenvalue problems, including methods for classification and dimensionality reduction. This paper studies a formulation that limits how many components can be nonzero, with sparse principal component analysis as a special case. In sparse PCA, the goal is to explain substantial variation using principal directions that involve relatively few variables.

Earlier approaches approximated the constraint on the number of nonzero components with an ℓ₁ norm. The authors propose a tighter approximation related to the negative log-likelihood of a Student's t-distribution. They express the resulting optimization as a difference-of-convex-functions program and solve it through a sequence of locally convex programs.

Across datasets of different dimensionalities, the method explains more variance with sparse loadings and scales better than comparison methods. Two experiments use high-dimensional gene datasets, where the objective is to identify a small set of relevant genes that explains as much variance as possible. These findings connect the revised sparsity approximation to both representation quality and computational behavior in the evaluated problems.
icml-2007-sparse-eigen-methods-by-d-c-pr.tldr: A tighter sparsity approximation and difference-of-convex optimization improve explained variance and scalability in sparse eigenvalue experiments.

paragraphs: Supervised feature selection asks which input information should be retained for predicting known targets. This paper proposes using statistical dependence between features and labels as the selection principle. It measures that relationship with the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, or HSIC, and seeks features that maximize the measured dependence.

The framework brings classification and regression into the same formulation. Rather than defining a separate selection principle for each kind of prediction target, it uses dependence as their common criterion. This focuses feature filtering on how the retained inputs relate to the supervised information available in the labels.

The authors approximate solutions using backward elimination, which progressively removes features from the candidate set. This supplies a practical procedure for applying the dependence-based objective. Tests on artificial and real-world datasets demonstrate the method's usefulness. The contribution is the combination of a shared statistical criterion, applicability across supervised learning problems, and an approximate selection algorithm; the reported evidence supports its utility without claiming that it universally identifies the best feature subset.
icml-2007-supervised-feature-selection-v.tldr: HSIC-based feature selection uses dependence on labels as a common objective for classification and regression.
